slides.title: The first conversation
slides.lead: Day 2: a Zillow Preferred lead arrives. What happens next?
slides.body:
A buyer asks about a home.
How do you help?

We’ll work from the lead alert through the first call and the next step you agree together.
slides.notes: Welcome the group. Connect to Day 1: they learned where work belongs in FUB. Today they will learn what to say and do when the lead arrives. Introduce yourself and explain that the examples use fictional buyers. Handoff: Yesterday we worked inside the record. Today we’ll work through the conversation that gives that record meaning. Sources: Eric’s September 14 Day 2 objective. All buyers and property details in examples are fictional.
slides.cue: Yesterday we worked inside the record. Today we’ll work through the conversation that gives that record meaning.

slides.title: The route through today’s session
slides.lead: We’ll follow Jordan’s request, then try a few clearly marked variations.
slides.body:
1. Receipt and first response

    Read the request, choose the contact method, then submit a vote and a text.

  2. The first conversation

    Watch the opening and discovery. Practice a follow-up with a partner.

  3. Questions, closing, and a full call

    Handle a buyer’s question, agree the plan, then rotate through a complete call.

You answer on the current slide in your own session. Submit, then we’ll discuss. The presenter advances everyone together.
slides.notes: Explain the 90-minute plan and two speaking practices. Ask everyone to open their learner session now. Explain that the first vote is also a connection check: pause there until actual responses arrive. Do not claim attendance alone proves submission works. Handoff: Let’s start where the agent starts: the request that just arrived. Sources: September 14 objective. All buyers and property details in examples are fictional.
slides.cue: Let’s start where the agent starts: the request that just arrived.

slides.title: The request tells you how to begin
slides.lead: Our example: Jordan asks to see 1234 Lane on Saturday morning.
slides.body:
Lead routeWhat you receiveWhat to check
Connection / contact agentA question about a home, live or by FUB alertThe question and contact preference
Real-time touringA tour alert using ShowingTime availabilityThe selected time and current arrangements
Standard tourA tour request, live or by FUB alertWhether the requested time is available

Jordan’s is a standard tour request. Saturday morning is the buyer’s preference. Property access still needs checking.
slides.notes: Explain each route through the decision it changes. Real-time touring does not arrive as a live call in Eric’s documented flow. Read actual timeframe and representation answers when supplied; a form question is not the buyer’s answer. Demonstrate: “I saw Saturday morning. I’ll check access and confirm with you.” Handoff: Before we contact Jordan, let’s check that distinction between a requested time and confirmed access. Sources: INT-012; documented TRU operating flow. All buyers and property details in examples are fictional.
slides.cue: Before we contact Jordan, let’s check that distinction between a requested time and confirmed access.

slides.title: Your turn: requested or confirmed?
slides.lead: Another standard tour lead asks for 5 p.m. Access is unconfirmed. What do you do?
slides.body:
Compare with the teaching example

Acknowledge 5 p.m., check access, and tell the buyer when you will confirm. Their request gives you a starting point; it does not prove the seller approved it.

Use the requested time while keeping an unverified arrangement separate from a confirmed appointment.
slides.notes: Allow 45 seconds for the vote. Verify submissions reach your presenter view. Ask one agent why they chose their answer. Reveal the explanation and emphasize that acknowledging a preference does not promise access. If answers do not arrive, resolve the join/submission problem before continuing. Handoff: We know what needs checking. Now we need to decide how to reach the buyer. Sources: TRU Sales Proccess; application of the preceding instruction. All buyers and property details in examples are fictional.
slides.cue: We know what needs checking. Now we need to decide how to reach the buyer.

activity.prompt: Another standard tour lead asks for 5 p.m. Access is unconfirmed. What do you do?
activity.model: Acknowledge 5 p.m., check access, and tell the buyer when you will confirm. Their request gives you a starting point; it does not prove the seller approved it.
activity.explanation: Use the requested time while keeping an unverified arrangement separate from a confirmed appointment.

choices.text: Confirm 5 p.m. now and check access afterward.
Acknowledge 5 p.m. and verify property access.
Ask for a new time before checking the requested one.

slides.title: How will you contact the buyer?
slides.lead: Back to Jordan: an alert arrived, with no special contact instruction.
slides.body:
Already on a live call

Introduce yourself and begin.

FUB alert, no preference

Call within five minutes of receipt during TRU’s 8 a.m.–8 p.m. operating window.

A specific instruction

Use the requested channel or callback time. Acknowledge a later callback by text now.
slides.notes: Point to Jordan’s alert example and choose the default call. Explain why: a conversation lets the agent hear the buyer and respond to their answers. Distinguish the automated introduction from the agent’s own call. Do not invent an after-hours deadline. Handoff: Let’s try that call. First, what happens if Jordan doesn’t pick up? Sources: R008–R010; INT-009–INT-013, INT-054. All buyers and property details in examples are fictional.
slides.cue: Let’s try that call. First, what happens if Jordan doesn’t pick up?

slides.title: Jordan does not answer
slides.lead: Your personal text connects the missed call to the original request.
slides.body:
While unanswered

Day one: aim for 3–4 personal touches, including at least 2 calls and 1 text. First week: 10 total including day one, mostly calls.

When Jordan replies

Continue from the reply and agree a plan. The unanswered-lead quota stops.
slides.notes: Read the text aloud. Explain the recognizable property, reason for calling, and genuine times offered. Mention an opening voicemail when appropriate. Automation is separate from personal effort. These are normal-flow targets, not an invented late-day schedule, and a stated contact restriction governs. Handoff: That was the default with no preference. Now change one fact: the buyer has told us when to call. Sources: R009, R019. All buyers and property details in examples are fictional.
slides.cue: That was the default with no preference. Now change one fact: the buyer has told us when to call.

slides.title: A requested callback changes the response
slides.lead: Variation: Maya is at work and asks for a call at five.
slides.body:
Text first for now

Help by text now. Offer a later call if useful.

An explicit no-call request

Honor it. Continue through the agreed channel.
slides.notes: Make the contrast explicit: Jordan gave no contact instruction; Maya did. Read the acknowledgment. The five-minute default does not justify ignoring her requested time. Offering an earlier call is optional and must reflect real availability. Text-first now is different from a permanent no-call instruction. Handoff: You’ve heard an acknowledgment. Write your own version for Maya. Sources: R008, R010; INT-013, INT-043. All buyers and property details in examples are fictional.
slides.cue: You’ve heard an acknowledgment. Write your own version for Maya.

slides.title: Your turn: acknowledge Maya
slides.lead: Maya’s alert arrives at 2 p.m. and asks for a 5 p.m. call. Write your acknowledgment.
slides.body:
Compare with the teaching example

Hi Maya, I’m Sam with Northside Realty. I’ll be calling at five about your inquiry. If you have a question before then, let me know. I’m also free earlier if that would help.

Introduce yourself promptly, keep the requested call time, and offer earlier availability only if it is real. Do not call immediately just to satisfy the normal five-minute default.
slides.notes: Give 60 seconds to write and submit. Read two responses, noticing whether each introduces the agent and preserves five o’clock. Reveal the example. Do not turn a difference in wording into an error if the meaning is accurate. Handoff: Now return to Jordan. The call connects. What should the conversation accomplish? Sources: TRU Sales Proccess; application of the preceding instruction. All buyers and property details in examples are fictional.
slides.cue: Now return to Jordan. The call connects. What should the conversation accomplish?

activity.prompt: Maya’s alert arrives at 2 p.m. and asks for a 5 p.m. call. Write your acknowledgment.

fields.label: What would you text Maya now?

activity.model: Hi Maya, I’m Sam with Northside Realty. I’ll be calling at five about your inquiry. If you have a question before then, let me know. I’m also free earlier if that would help.
activity.explanation: Introduce yourself promptly, keep the requested call time, and offer earlier availability only if it is real. Do not call immediately just to satisfy the normal five-minute default.

slides.title: Jordan answers. Where does the call go?
slides.lead: Introduce yourself first. ALMS gives the conversation a direction.
slides.body:
A

Appointment

Help with the requested visit.

L

Location

Learn where they want to be.

M

Motivation

Learn why it matters.

S

Summarize

Agree what happens next.

Location and motivation can come in either order. The buyer’s answers guide the next question.
slides.notes: Give the whole route before demonstrating pieces. Explain that the appointment invitation comes early because the buyer asked for help with a home. ALMS should help the agent listen, not become a list to recite. Handoff: Here is the first part aloud: an introduction that leads directly into Jordan’s request. Sources: R012–R013; INT-015–INT-016. All buyers and property details in examples are fictional.
slides.cue: Here is the first part aloud: an introduction that leads directly into Jordan’s request.

slides.title: The opening answers “Who is this?”
slides.lead: Jordan requested Saturday morning. Use that information.
slides.body:
Agent “Hi Jordan, I’m Sam with Northside Realty, a featured partner with Zillow. I’m calling about your request to see 1234 Lane.”

Agent “I saw Saturday morning. I’ll check access for that time. Would morning still work for you?”

Jordan “Yes, morning works.”

No time selected? Offer two times you can actually make. Property access still needs confirmation.
slides.notes: Read both sides. Pause after the introduction to identify name, brokerage, Zillow connection, and purpose. Then demonstrate the early invitation. On a live transfer, say Zillow connected you about the request. Use the real affiliation and available times. Never borrow an invented expertise claim. Handoff: Now try the same opening skill with one change: no tour time was selected. Sources: R013; INT-016. All buyers and property details in examples are fictional.
slides.cue: Now try the same opening skill with one change: no tour time was selected.

slides.title: Your turn: no time was selected
slides.lead: Practice variation: Jordan asked to see 1234 Lane but selected no time. How would you begin?
slides.body:
Compare with the teaching example

Hi Jordan, I’m Sam with Northside Realty, a featured partner with Zillow. I’m calling about your request to see 1234 Lane. Would Saturday morning or afternoon work better? I’ll verify access for the time we choose.

Orient the buyer and offer useful times before discovery. Use actual availability. The invitation is a strong default, not a reason to ignore a buyer’s stated circumstances.
slides.notes: Give 90 seconds to choose and write. Discuss one opening that connects naturally to the inquiry. The invitation should precede a qualification interview, while preserving uncertain access. Reveal the example after responses. Say explicitly that this was a variation; the main example returns to Saturday morning next. Handoff: Back in our main call, Jordan prefers Saturday morning. We have a starting plan, but we still know very little about Jordan. Sources: TRU Sales Proccess; application of the preceding instruction. All buyers and property details in examples are fictional.
slides.cue: Back in our main call, Jordan prefers Saturday morning. We have a starting plan, but we still know very little about Jordan.

activity.prompt: Practice variation: Jordan asked to see 1234 Lane but selected no time. How would you begin?

fields.label: Write your introduction and early appointment invitation.

activity.model: Hi Jordan, I’m Sam with Northside Realty, a featured partner with Zillow. I’m calling about your request to see 1234 Lane. Would Saturday morning or afternoon work better? I’ll verify access for the time we choose.
activity.explanation: Orient the buyer and offer useful times before discovery. Use actual availability. The invitation is a strong default, not a reason to ignore a buyer’s stated circumstances.

choices.text: Ask about budget and preapproval before offering a time.
Explain the buying process before discussing the visit.
Introduce yourself and offer workable showing times.

slides.title: The appointment opens a conversation
slides.lead: Before asking about the search, explain why the questions help.
slides.body:
Agent “Do you have a few minutes so I can learn what you’re looking for and make our time together useful?”

Jordan “Sure. We’re already in town.”

Agent “What’s changing where you live now?”

Jordan “We rent an apartment. We’d like outdoor space.”

If they have only a minute, keep it brief. Handle the request and agreed next action without forcing a full interview.
slides.notes: Read the exchange. Ask aloud what the follow-up learned that “in town” alone did not tell us. Connect this to location: use their current situation and ask which areas work for them and why. Do not assume a lease end, children, or a reason for moving. Handoff: Jordan mentioned outdoor space. That gives us the next question. Sources: R013; INT-016, INT-023. All buyers and property details in examples are fictional.
slides.cue: Jordan mentioned outdoor space. That gives us the next question.

slides.title: “Outdoor space” needs a follow-up
slides.lead: The feature becomes useful when you understand its purpose.
slides.body:
Agent “What would you like to do with that space?”

Jordan “I’d like a vegetable garden.”

Agent “What would you need from the space for that?”

Jordan “Somewhere sunny, with room for raised beds.”

Now the search has a reason: usable garden space. A large yard alone may not solve it.
slides.notes: Read each turn and point to the link between the answer and the next question. Briefly contrast “Great, how many bedrooms?” which abandons the answer. Use authentic warmth without a memorized personal anecdote. Ask the room what they now know they did not know before. Handoff: You’ve heard a follow-up reveal the reason. Practice finding the reason with a partner. Sources: R013; INT-016, INT-021. All buyers and property details in examples are fictional.
slides.cue: You’ve heard a follow-up reveal the reason. Practice finding the reason with a partner.

slides.title: Partner practice: what does “more space” mean?
slides.lead: Practice variation: your buyer says, “We need more space.” Learn what that means, then switch roles.
slides.body:
1. First turn: 3 minutes

    Ask permission, follow the buyer’s answer, then use one correction to retry.

  2. Switch buyer and agent: 3 minutes

    Use a new reason for needing more space. Everyone gets a speaking turn.

  3. Room debrief: 1 minute

    Share the follow-up that taught you something useful.

1 minute to set up. Video rooms are in your meeting platform. Submit your reflection after practice.

Compare with the teaching example

“What is feeling too tight in your current place?” Their answer could reveal the purpose of the space. Follow that answer rather than assuming a larger bedroom count solves it.

Choose a question connected to the buyer’s words. There is no required question count, personal anecdote, or fixed order for location and motivation.
slides.notes: 8 minutes: 1 minute setup, 3 minutes each direction (2-minute conversation and 1-minute correction/retry), 1-minute debrief. Assign speaking turns and open the meeting platform’s rooms. Buyer invents a simple reason and reveals it when asked. Listen for permission and a question connected to the actual answer. On return, ask one pair what changed on the retry. Handoff: You have a way to learn what matters. Before we close the call, let’s handle questions that can interrupt that plan. Sources: TRU Sales Proccess; application of the preceding instruction. All buyers and property details in examples are fictional.
slides.cue: You have a way to learn what matters. Before we close the call, let’s handle questions that can interrupt that plan.

activity.prompt: Practice variation: your buyer says, “We need more space.” Learn what that means, then switch roles.

fields.label: What would you ask next, and what would that help you understand?
What did your partner suggest, and how did your retry change?

activity.model: “What is feeling too tight in your current place?” Their answer could reveal the purpose of the space. Follow that answer rather than assuming a larger bedroom count solves it.
activity.explanation: Choose a question connected to the buyer’s words. There is no required question count, personal anecdote, or fixed order for location and motivation.

rubric.label: Ask a follow-up based on the buyer’s actual answer

slides.title: What if the buyer only wants an answer?
slides.lead: Variation: the buyer declines a tour and asks about the roof.
slides.body:
Agent “Of course. What would you like to know?”

Buyer “How old is the roof?”

Agent “I’ll check that. Can I ask what concerns you about it?”

Buyer “I’m worried about taking on repairs.”

Bring the answer back. Explain how a viewing could help them decide. If they still decline, agree how to return the information.
slides.notes: Make clear this is an alternate buyer response, not a new fact about Jordan. Demonstrate a useful second invitation: “Seeing it could help you decide whether it fits, and I can bring the roof answer. Would that be useful?” If declined, stop pushing and arrange the answer. Answer known facts now. Do not make information conditional on meeting. Handoff: A property question can reveal a concern. The same applies when the buyer asks about financing. Sources: R014; INT-016. All buyers and property details in examples are fictional.
slides.cue: A property question can reveal a concern. The same applies when the buyer asks about financing.

slides.title: When the buyer asks about a lender
slides.lead: Variation: “Should I talk to a lender before we look?”
slides.body:
Agent “A lender can help you understand your options. What are you hoping to work out before we look?”

Buyer “I don’t know what payment I’d be comfortable with.”

Agent “That’s useful to work through. I can help connect you with a lender to discuss those numbers.”

Help with the concern. Do not turn the showing request into a demand for preapproval.
slides.notes: Read the example. The buyer introduced financing, so address it. Explain that lender-specific numbers belong with the lender. Eric’s usual later opening is the end of the first showing; today covers the buyer-raised first-call question only. Do not lecture on loan products. Handoff: Choose the response that helps with that concern while keeping the meeting easy. Sources: R001–R004; INT-001–INT-005, INT-016. All buyers and property details in examples are fictional.
slides.cue: Choose the response that helps with that concern while keeping the meeting easy.

slides.title: Your turn: a financing question
slides.lead: The buyer asks, “Should I talk to a lender before we look?” What is the best response?
slides.body:
Compare with the teaching example

“A lender can help you understand your options. What are you hoping to work out before we look?” If they need help with payments or financing options, offer a lender connection.

Buyer-initiated financing questions deserve an answer. Avoid both a blanket refusal to discuss money and a blanket requirement to obtain preapproval before receiving help.
slides.notes: Allow a short vote, then ask someone to say the answer in everyday language. Reveal and discuss why both refusing the topic and imposing a blanket preapproval gate miss the buyer’s question. Handoff: Another question may be about who you represent. Keep that answer just as direct. Sources: TRU Sales Proccess; application of the preceding instruction. All buyers and property details in examples are fictional.
slides.cue: Another question may be about who you represent. Keep that answer just as direct.

activity.prompt: The buyer asks, “Should I talk to a lender before we look?” What is the best response?
activity.model: “A lender can help you understand your options. What are you hoping to work out before we look?” If they need help with payments or financing options, offer a lender connection.
activity.explanation: Buyer-initiated financing questions deserve an answer. Avoid both a blanket refusal to discuss money and a blanket requirement to obtain preapproval before receiving help.

choices.text: Ask what they need to work out, then offer relevant lender help.
Save the financing question for the showing and move on.
Ask for a preapproval letter before scheduling the showing.

slides.title: “Are you the listing agent?”
slides.lead: The buyer needs a clear answer about your role.
slides.body: If they prefer the listing agent, offer to help with that connection. Respect their choice.
slides.notes: Read the short answer and return to the property question. Use the real role. If an existing representation agreement raises an unresolved question, involve the team lead using the actual circumstances and form. Avoid an agency lecture. Handoff: Your role is clear. Now suppose the answer about the property itself is disappointing. Sources: R015; INT-016–INT-018. All buyers and property details in examples are fictional.
slides.cue: Your role is clear. Now suppose the answer about the property itself is disappointing.

slides.title: The home is under contract
slides.lead: Separate variation: you learn this during the first inquiry. No showing is confirmed.
slides.body:
Agent “The home is under contract. I can check whether a viewing is still possible. What drew you to it?”

Buyer “The yard. I want room for a garden.”

Agent “I can also research homes with useful garden space. Would that help?”

State what you know. Keep access and unresearched alternatives conditional.
slides.notes: Apply Eric’s problem-solving principle only to this first-call scenario. We are not teaching a cancellation or showing-day workflow. Explain why the next step uses the buyer’s reason. Do not claim to have researched alternatives when you have not. Handoff: Try giving that news with a specific next step tied to what the buyer told you. Sources: R011–R012 applied to the initial availability question. All buyers and property details in examples are fictional.
slides.cue: Try giving that news with a specific next step tied to what the buyer told you.

slides.title: Your turn: a home under contract
slides.lead: Variation: the home is under contract. The buyer wants garden space. What do you say next?
slides.body:
Compare with the teaching example

“The home is under contract. I can check whether a viewing is still possible. Since garden space matters, I can also research some options to compare. Would that be useful?” Keep access and unresearched alternatives conditional.

Tell the truth, use known priorities, keep possibilities conditional, and offer a next step. Do not merely hand the search back with “Want something else?”
slides.notes: Give 60 seconds for writing. Compare one bare status update with one truthful plan tied to garden space. Reveal after responses. Listen for unsupported promises about access or already-researched alternatives. Handoff: Those were alternate situations. Return to Jordan’s original call: Saturday morning is preferred, garden space matters, and access is still pending. Sources: TRU Sales Proccess; application of the preceding instruction. All buyers and property details in examples are fictional.
slides.cue: Those were alternate situations. Return to Jordan’s original call: Saturday morning is preferred, garden space matters, and access is still pending.

activity.prompt: Variation: the home is under contract. The buyer wants garden space. What do you say next?

fields.label: Write your response and a useful next step.

activity.model: “The home is under contract. I can check whether a viewing is still possible. Since garden space matters, I can also research some options to compare. Would that be useful?” Keep access and unresearched alternatives conditional.
activity.explanation: Tell the truth, use known priorities, keep possibilities conditional, and offer a next step. Do not merely hand the search back with “Want something else?”

slides.title: The plan should use what Jordan told you
slides.lead: Back to the original call. Jordan wants sunny space for raised beds.
slides.body:
Agent “Would it help to compare another home with usable garden space while we’re out?”

Jordan “Yes, that would help.”

Agent “Saturday morning is your preference. I’ll check access to 1234 Lane and research a comparison with garden space. I’ll text you the details after I hear back. Is that right?”

Jordan “Yes. Text is good.”
slides.notes: Demonstrate obtaining agreement before adding comparisons. Explain Eric’s goal of two or three homes without making extra homes a condition. The summary reflects actual priorities, permission, pending checks, and the agreed channel. Briefly explain the applicable touring form and what you will send, using its actual terms. Do not invent signing status. Handoff: Now close that call in your own words, using only what Jordan has agreed to. Sources: R013; INT-016. All buyers and property details in examples are fictional.
slides.cue: Now close that call in your own words, using only what Jordan has agreed to.

slides.title: Your turn: the agreed next step
slides.lead: Jordan wants garden space, prefers Saturday morning, accepts a comparison home, and agrees to text. Access is pending.
slides.body:
Compare with the teaching example

“Garden space matters, and Saturday morning is your preference. I’ll check access and research a comparison with room for a garden. I’ll text you the details after I hear back. Have I missed anything?”

Do not upgrade a requested time into a confirmed showing. Reflect the actual priorities and your promised action.
slides.notes: Give 60 seconds to submit. Ask which parts are agreed and which remain pending. Reveal and discuss. A useful close can be brief; it must preserve the buyer’s facts and the agent’s actual commitment. Handoff: You’ve practiced the parts. Watch how those same parts connect in one uninterrupted call. Sources: TRU Sales Proccess; application of the preceding instruction. All buyers and property details in examples are fictional.
slides.cue: You’ve practiced the parts. Watch how those same parts connect in one uninterrupted call.

activity.prompt: Jordan wants garden space, prefers Saturday morning, accepts a comparison home, and agrees to text. Access is pending.

fields.label: Write the summary and next step you would say aloud.

activity.model: “Garden space matters, and Saturday morning is your preference. I’ll check access and research a comparison with room for a garden. I’ll text you the details after I hear back. Have I missed anything?”
activity.explanation: Do not upgrade a requested time into a confirmed showing. Reflect the actual priorities and your promised action.

slides.title: The whole call: opening and discovery
slides.lead: Demonstration. Follow the conversation rather than naming each step.
slides.body:
Sam “Hi Jordan, I’m Sam with Northside Realty, a featured partner with Zillow. I’m calling about 1234 Lane. I saw Saturday morning. Would that still work? I’ll check access.”

Jordan “Yes, morning works.”

Sam “Have you got a few minutes so I can make our time useful?”

Jordan “Sure.”

Sam “What’s changing where you live now?”

Jordan “We rent in town. We’d like outdoor space.”
slides.notes: Ask a volunteer to read Jordan or read both parts yourself. Do not stop to label every ALMS letter. Agents listen for what each answer gives the agent to work with. Continue directly to the next slide without opening a new discussion. Handoff: Jordan has just said “outdoor space.” Continue from those words. Sources: R013; adapted from INT-016. All buyers and property details in examples are fictional.
slides.cue: Jordan has just said “outdoor space.” Continue from those words.

slides.title: The same call: discovery and agreement
slides.lead: Continue without restarting the conversation.
slides.body:
Sam “What would you like to do with that space?”

Jordan “A vegetable garden. I need sun and room for raised beds.”

Sam “Would comparing another home with garden space help?”

Jordan “Yes.”

Sam “Saturday morning is your preference. I’ll check access and research that comparison, then text the details. Does that work?”

Jordan “Yes, text is good.”
slides.notes: Finish the demonstration aloud. Briefly explain the applicable touring form and promised follow-up in accurate terms. Ask what made the next step specific to Jordan. Then give practice instructions; do not introduce another topic. Handoff: Now run a call yourselves. Keep the sequence, but respond to the buyer you actually hear. Sources: R012–R013, R016. All buyers and property details in examples are fictional.
slides.cue: Now run a call yourselves. Keep the sequence, but respond to the buyer you actually hear.

slides.title: Group practice: the complete first call
slides.lead: Trios rotate through agent, buyer, and observer. Everyone speaks.
slides.body:
1. Call: 3 minutes

    Use the buyer card. Introduce yourself, help with the request, follow answers, and agree a next step.

  2. Feedback and retry: 1 minute

    Observer names one moment. Agent replays that part.

  3. Rotate, then debrief

    Repeat until all three have spoken. Submit the reflection after your turn.

1 minute setup, three 4-minute rounds, 2-minute debrief. Your assigned roles appear in your session. Video rooms are in your meeting platform.

Compare with the teaching example

Introduce yourself, offer the appointment early, ask permission, explore location and motivation through follow-up questions, and summarize the actual plan. Adapt if Jordan has limited time or a different request.

Use a partner as the buyer. When studying alone, say the agent’s turns aloud and compare with the two demonstration slides. A self-check is practice, not observed coach sign-off.
slides.notes: 15 minutes: 1 minute setup, three 4-minute rounds (3-minute call and 1-minute correction/retry), 2-minute debrief. Assign speaking turns, then use the meeting platform’s rooms. Buyer uses the assigned card and reveals the underlying reason in conversation. Observer gives one concrete correction. On return, ask which buyer answer changed the agent’s next question. A simulated or peer check is not coach sign-off. Handoff: The call is finished. Your next action should make good on the promise you just made. Sources: TRU Sales Proccess; application of the preceding instruction. All buyers and property details in examples are fictional.
slides.cue: The call is finished. Your next action should make good on the promise you just made.

activity.prompt: Trios rotate through agent, buyer, and observer. Everyone speaks.

fields.label: What did you learn about the buyer?
What changed when you tried it again?

rubric.label: Clear name, brokerage, Zillow connection and purpose
Useful early appointment invitation that respects the request
Permission, relevant location/motivation questions and a follow-up
Accurate priorities, commitments and unresolved checks
Responds to the buyer’s actual preference and circumstances

slides.title: The record should match the call
slides.lead: Day 1 showed where to save the work. Here is what Jordan’s call gives you.
slides.body:
Conversation note

Rents locally. Wants sunny space for raised beds. Prefers Saturday morning. Open to a comparison home. Text agreed.

Pending action

Check access to 1234 Lane and research a useful comparison.

Task and next contact

Set a task for the promised work. Text the details after the access answer, as agreed.

Saturday morning remains requested until access is confirmed. Do not record a completed showing or an agreement the buyer did not make.
slides.notes: Connect directly to the note and task skills from Day 1. Read the example record against the call. slides.title: Your first-call reference
slides.lead: Read the request. Help with it. Agree what happens next.
slides.body:
Before contact

Check the lead route, home, requested time, and contact preference.

When connected

Introduce yourself. Offer the appointment early. Ask permission, then follow the buyer’s answers about location and motivation.

Before finishing

Summarize priorities, pending checks, and the agreed next action. Save the note and task.

Open the examples and first-call reference

cases.name: Jordan · a garden
cases.quote: I’d like to see 1234 Lane Saturday morning. The yard caught my eye.
cases.goal: Buyer: you rent locally and want sun and room for raised beds. Reveal those details after relevant questions. You are open to a comparison home. Access remains unconfirmed.

cases.name: Maya · text first
cases.quote: I’m at work. Please text me now; I can talk at five.
cases.goal: Begin with the text exchange, then fast-forward to the agreed call. Buyer: a shorter commute matters; reveal it when asked. Honor the contact preference and agree the later conversation.

cases.name: Alex · questions first
cases.quote: I only wanted to know about the roof. I’m not ready to book a showing.
cases.goal: Buyer: maintenance costs concern you. Reveal this after a relevant question. Decline the next invitation too. Agent should help with the question and agree how to return verified information.
